# Harbour: a streaming CSV importer for order records

Harbour is a command-line tool for importing order records from CSV files into an existing ledger.

The main change from the old importer is how the file is read. The old importer loaded the whole file into memory before doing any work, so memory use scaled with file size. A 2 GB file was loaded in full. Harbour reads the file in chunks of 8,000 rows using a streaming parser, and distributes work across 4 workers. Memory use stays flat regardless of how large the file is.

## Validate before you write

Harbour validates each record before writing it. Records that fail validation are written to an error file along with their line number and the column name that failed. Records that pass are still imported, so one bad row does not abort the run or block the other 199,999 rows in the file.

Under the old importer, a few rows with a malformed date, a missing identifier or a stray value in a numeric column would fail the job; you would fix one row and run it again. Harbour imports what is valid and leaves the failures in the error report.

A dry run validates without writing:

```
harbour import orders.csv --dry-run
```

This validates the whole file and writes the error report, but does not write anything to the ledger. Use it when a new file format arrives, or when an upstream system changes and you want to know what broke before it reaches production.

## Retries and checkpoints

A normal import reuses the `order_id` from the source record rather than generating a new identifier. The ledger ignores duplicate identifiers, so re-running an import that was interrupted will not produce duplicate entries.

This protects against duplicates on retry. It does not repair an incorrect source record: if a record was written with a wrong value and you fix the CSV and re-import, the ledger will see the same `order_id` and ignore the new version. Correcting already-imported data is a separate problem that Harbour does not solve.

Harbour also records a checkpoint after each completed chunk. If the process is interrupted, the next run resumes from the last completed checkpoint instead of starting over.

## Benchmarks

In a local test across 35 files of up to 2 GB:

| | Harbour | Old importer |
|---|---|---|
| Median import time | 4.8 s | 6.2 s |
| Peak memory | 72 MB | 1.1 GB |

The time improvement is modest. Peak memory fell from 1.1 GB to 72 MB, which decouples memory use from file size.

The numbers come from a single Linux machine with a local SSD. Network storage or different row lengths may behave differently, and the test did not measure what happens when multiple import jobs run at the same time. If you run concurrent imports, measure that yourself.

## Limitations

Small files may be slower than under the old importer. Starting 4 workers and opening the checkpoint store both add fixed overhead, which a small file does not amortise. We do not have small-file timings to quantify this, so if your workload is mostly small files, benchmark before switching.

The supported encoding is UTF-8. Embedded newlines in quoted fields are handled correctly. Files in other encodings must be converted before import; Harbour will not do the conversion for you.

Harbour is a command-line tool. There is no web interface, no schema editor, and no remote scheduling service. It is intended to be driven by whatever you already use to run jobs.

## Rollout advice

Start with a dry run against a copy of representative data:

```
harbour import orders.csv --dry-run
```

Then work through the error report. Rows that fail here were handled somehow by the old importer, so establish how before you change behaviour in production. Compare the set of accepted records against what the old importer produces on the same input, and if the counts differ, find out why.

Verify duplicate handling explicitly before enabling production writes. Run an import, interrupt it, resume it, and confirm the ledger contains what you expect.

Once dry runs are clean and duplicate handling is confirmed on your data, enable production writes.
